transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hi Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you too. So, um, I guess I'm here because... well, it's been building up for a little while, but what finally pushed me to actually make the appointment and come in today is this thing I keep doing where I just cannot seem to stay in my chair. 

I'm a software developer, so a lot of my day is at a desk, and we have these really long sprint planning meetings. They're super important, you know, because we're mapping out the entire next two weeks of work for the whole team, and I know I need to be present and at my desk for them. But I just... I keep getting up. Even when I know I absolutely should stay put and look at the screen, I'll just suddenly feel like I have to move. Like, I'll be sitting there, and someone is explaining a complex ticket, and I'll suddenly think, "I need a glass of water right this exact second," or I'll just randomly decide I need to go check something in the other room, like if I left my notebook on the counter or something completely trivial that could definitely wait.

And it's not just work, either! It happens in my personal life too. I've been having these really serious mortgage calls lately, and you'd think for something involving that much money and paperwork I could just sit in my chair for thirty minutes and focus, but no, I'm wandering off to the kitchen while the loan officer is in the middle of explaining interest rates. It's just so frustrating because I know in my head, "sit down, stay here, this is important," but I'm already out of the chair before I've even fully processed it. So, yeah, that's really the main thing that made me realize I should probably come in and talk to someone.
Looking back at your life, did you experience these same difficulties with sitting still and staying focused when you were a child, or is this something that only started more recently?

Oh, wow, um, looking back... yeah. Yeah, it's definitely not a new thing, not at all. It's actually kind of funny you ask that because just the other day I was thinking about how much trouble I used to get into when I was a kid. Like, in elementary school, I remember this one specific teacher—Mrs. Gable, I think it was third grade—she actually had to move my desk right up next to hers. And not because I was struggling with the material! I actually understood the work fine, usually. But I just could not stay in my seat. I was always popping up to go sharpen a pencil, or to look out the window, or to see what the kid three rows over was drawing. 

And it wasn't just the getting up, either. I was constantly blurting things out. Like, the teacher would ask a question, and before she even finished the sentence, I was just saying the answer out loud without raising my hand. I remember her saying, over and over, "Raise your hand, wait to be called on," but it was like the thought would pop into my head and just immediately come out of my mouth before I could stop it. I was always rushing through my worksheets, too. I'd just speed through them, make a bunch of careless mistakes even though I knew the answers, just so I could be done and move on to something else. So, yeah, I guess when I really think about it, I've always been like this. It's just that now, as a forty-year-old adult, it's a lot less acceptable to just wander around the room during a meeting than it was during third-grade math, you know? But the feeling—that urge to just get up and do something else—that's been there for as long as I can remember.

Beyond the physical restlessness and impulsivity you've described, do you often find that you struggle with losing things, being forgetful in daily activities, or having difficulty organizing tasks and keeping track of your belongings?

Oh, gosh, yes. Organization is... well, it's a whole other ordeal. It's actually kind of a running joke at this point, except it's really not funny because it drives me absolutely crazy. I feel like I'm constantly trying to build these perfect systems to keep myself organized, and they just completely fall apart the second I try to use them. 

Like, okay, take my day-to-day tasks. I have my work tickets—the ones we talk about in those endless sprint planning meetings I mentioned—and you'd think I'd just keep track of them in our project management software like a normal person, right? But no, I'll have a random thought about a piece of code, and I'll drop a note in my own personal Slack channel. Then later, I'm on a call, and I'll jot down something about my home repair notes—because we're trying to fix up the guest bathroom right now, which is a whole separate headache with the plumbing—and I'll write that on a neon pink sticky note and just slap it onto the bottom bezel of my monitor. And then I have these budget reminders, especially with the mortgage refinancing stuff I was telling you about, and those get shoved into an email draft, or maybe I set a vague alarm on my phone that just says "call bank" with no other context. 

So I end up with this absolute tornado of information. Everything I need to function is just completely scattered between Slack, a million sticky notes all over my desk, my email inbox, and random apps on my phone. And what happens is, I sit down at my desk, and I spend more time just trying to figure out what I was supposed to do—like, hunting down which app or which scrap of paper has the actual next step on it—than I spend actually doing the task itself! It’s exhausting, honestly. I’ll spend thirty minutes just cross-referencing a sticky note with a Slack thread, and by the time I piece together what the work ticket even was, I've completely lost the momentum to actually write the code. So, yeah, keeping track of tasks is definitely a massive struggle for me.

Do you find that you frequently struggle to sustain your attention on tasks or conversations for long periods, leading to you making careless mistakes or missing details, even when you are managing to stay in your seat?

Oh, completely. Yes. It's like... even if I manage to win the battle of physically staying in my chair, which, like I said, is a massive struggle on its own, my brain just decides to get up and walk away instead. 

Like, I can sit down and start reviewing a pull request for work—and code reviews are so crucial, you really have to pay attention to the logic and make sure nothing is going to break the build—or, you know, reading through those endless, dense mortgage documents for the refinance I mentioned earlier. And I go into it with such good intentions! I'll literally tell myself, "Okay, we are going to read this, we are going to focus, we are going to get this done." And I am looking right at the screen. I am sitting still. 

But then, I don't know, maybe three or four minutes go by, and suddenly I'll realize that I am just... staring at the exact same section. My eyes are technically scanning the words or the block of code, but I haven't absorbed a single piece of information because my mind is just completely gone. I'll be sitting there thinking about five totally unrelated things all at once. I'll be wondering if the plumber is actually going to call me back about the guest bathroom, which makes me think about whether I need to buy new towels to match the new tile, and then I'm suddenly remembering an email I forgot to reply to yesterday, and wondering what I should thaw out for dinner... all while I'm supposedly reading a legally binding financial document or checking someone's code!

And you asked about careless mistakes, and yes, that is exactly what happens because of this. Because I'll *think* I read it, right? I've been staring at it long enough! So I'll just sign the form, or I'll click 'approve' on the pull request, and then later another developer will point out this glaring, obvious bug that was right in front of my face. Or the loan officer will email me back saying I missed a whole section of signatures. And then I have to go back and force myself to re-read the same paragraph like six times just to actually comprehend what it says. It's incredibly frustrating because I *want* to pay attention, I really, really do, and I know the details matter, but it’s like my attention span just evaporates into thin air without me even noticing it's happening.
When you look back at your childhood, did you struggle more with the hyperactivity and impulsive behaviors, or was the difficulty with focus and attention just as significant back then?

Oh, that's a really interesting question. You know, trying to weigh which one was actually worse back then... it's tough. I honestly couldn't tell you. I really don't know if one was more significant than the other, because when you're a kid, you know, seven or eight years old, you don't exactly have the self-awareness to sit there and analyze your own cognitive processes, right? Like, I wasn't sitting at my desk thinking, "Ah, my sustained attention is wandering." I just knew I was in trouble again. 

It's all just this big blur of constantly being redirected. Because on the one hand, the physical stuff—the moving around—was just so visible. Like I mentioned with Mrs. Gable and moving my desk, that was the stuff that got adults frustrated. Teachers notice when a kid is physically out of their seat, or when they're talking over someone, or when they're practically vibrating with energy while everyone else is sitting criss-cross applesauce on the rug. So that got all the attention. But the focus part? I really don't know if it was just as bad back then or if it just flew under the radar because it's mostly invisible. 

Like, if I was staring out the window, was I failing to focus on the math lesson, or was I just bored? I honestly have no idea. And it's funny because when I try to picture it, I just remember the feeling of being completely swept up by everything around me. If the classroom was too loud, or the kid next to me was tapping a pencil, my brain would just latch onto that instead of the teacher. But was that me losing focus, or was that the impulsivity making me instantly react to the noise? I just don't know how to separate the two. They feel completely intertwined to me. 

Even now, trying to look back at it through an adult lens, I can't definitively say, "Oh yes, the attention issues were exactly as severe as the bouncing off the walls." Because maybe I was making all those careless mistakes on my worksheets because I couldn't sustain my focus, or maybe I was making them because I was just impulsively rushing so I could go play outside. It's like a chicken and egg situation, honestly. So, yeah, I really don't have a clear answer for which one was the bigger hurdle back then. They just both kind of fed into this giant, chaotic mess of a school experience, and I couldn't really tell you where one stopped and the other started.
